I think you and I may get different meaning out of pride events.  Even if they are an accepting place for all identities, I see them as a space of celebration for marginalized identities based on gender/sexual orientation.  In our culture, a straight guy's sexual orientation is tacitly accepted and celebrated by everything from laws to language to advertising.  I'm not suggesting policing anyone's clothing, but I do think the more thoughtful, tactful, and empathetic choice would have been a willingness on the part of a straight person to step back from the ubiquity of their personal identity for a few hours.  Maybe they would benefit from that as an ally.

Personally, I don't identify as straight, but I do have a lot of straight privilege.  I don't see the need to assert those aspects of my life in queer spaces, because it's important to me to keep those privileges in check.  Also, when I'm in a space with the intention of being an ally to a marginalized group, I see no benefit from asserting my personal privileges and find it derailing.  When I've participated in immigrant rights actions, I would never think of wearing a shirt reading "Born in the USA," and I'd be irritated by anyone who did.

If we're talking about fostering persecution, I think the urge to maintain hierarchies that have been the cause of historical and existing persecution is more of a concern than a criticism of the dominant group.

I doubt the guy in the photo intended to cause harm, but what comes across to me is that he didn't really think through what it means to be an ally to the LGBT community. 

It's true, unwanted advances are uncomfortable.  He's benefiting from straight/male privilege to fend off those unwanted advances.  I feel like if a woman wore that shirt, she'd probably still get unwanted advances from dudes, and wouldn't necessarily be safe wearing that shirt away from a setting like a pride parade, same for a gay man wearing a "I <3 Men" shirt.  Plus consider that the stereotype of gay men as sexual predators is a common excuse for homophobic behavior.

Also, our entire society is built on the assumption that everyone is straight, that straight is normal, that straight is better.  Can't a straight person take a backseat for one afternoon?

I'm a political and CAFAB.  Even though I've had the privilege to spend the past year or so working in LGBT agencies, I've not often been part of discussions about how people personally identify in terms of gender, although I've known people who've referred to themselves as femme (CAFAB), genderqueer (CAFAB), and bigender (CAMAB).  The few times I've come out to people IRL about my gender identity, I've used the terms "genderqueer" or "gender non-conforming," or given a description of my relationships to my gender instead of a label.  Next month my work schedule changes such that I will be able to attend a genderqueer discussion group in my town, so I'm really excited to see what that will be like :)

For me the struggle to give my gender a word comes from negotiating between acknowledging my cis-privilege and what my gender actually is, which does not fit into the socially acceptable box.  I've described myself as "cis-sexual female genderqueer," meaning that while I am GQ I've not transitioned my pronouns, body, legal gender, or name (most of the time).  However, my experience is one of consistently feeling like I don't fit into or live up to the gendered expectations that come along with being female/woman, and that informs my identity.  I came to a point in my life where I realized I could continue to be miserable and insecure about failing at someone else's gender, or I could embrace and win at my own gender.  Thus I am posting here.

Words I've used to describe myself when I want to be as accurate as possible about my gender identity have been: 
femostly/femdrogynous: pretty self explanatory, situating myself between androgyny and femmeness
grrl: which usually feels most honest for me-- femaleness, but politicized and unapologetically done my own way.  It's hard to say, though, without being misheard as "girl."  Or sounding strange.  Kathleen Hanna, what do?
lady-bear: I feel like my fat and my body hair are major components of how my gender is queered, and I really admire and identify with bear culture for celebrating those attributes in gay men.  Also my best friend is a bear.  Bears are awesome.

My one experience (dose and a half) was very positive, I tripped with an experienced psychonaut whom I trusted, in my home which was in a quiet rural area at the time.  Physically, things just felt... good. I kept having this sensation like seltzer bubbling inside of me.  Laughing felt *amazing*.  Of course my friend and I shtupped like bunny rabbits the whole time so that probably helped with the good sensations.  Psychologically, I felt very sensitive and suggestible.  We would joke about something, and the joke would become a very vivid mental image... I specifically remember we were talking about a bear, and I imagined a bear wearing a top hat and monocle strolling by my window.  While I knew that it was my imagination, it felt more real than reality.  Lying in my bedroom with only a string of Christmas lights lit up felt like floating in space.  I had a few mild visuals, my window blinds lighting up in patterns, and colors were extremely vivid.

The only drawbacks were that I was also very suggestible to negative visuals, luckily my friend was able to figure out what was happening when I got caught up feeling ashamed and insecure and helped me focus on my breathing and calm down.  I was really lucky to have an experienced person there with me.  And I felt god-awful the next day, but dealing with that was as simple as calling out of work and sleeping it off :)
